technique: verbs over adjectives — how the action words carry the weight
poem:
A crow throws two rough notes across the valley
and gets no answer back but its own echo,
thin off the far ridge where the maples stand
half-stripped now, the gold of them come loose
and drifting down to lie among the roots.
You hear it from your bed, that single bird,
the way a man hears something and stays still,
counting the quiet cost of one more day.
The stove's gone cold. The floor will test your feet.
But there's a kettle waiting to be filled,
and what you've started asks that you keep on—
not finished yet, not near, but under way.

The air out there's got that first cool bite to it, and it only comes this clear for a few short weeks.

So — up!
lesson: Today we work on one thing. Verbs. A verb is an action word. It tells you what something does. This poem leans on its verbs to do the work. Look at a crow throws two rough notes across the valley. The word throws does the labour there. Look at the gold of them come loose and drifting down. And look at the floor will test your feet. This works because an action word makes you picture a thing moving. Throws makes the crow's call feel hard and sudden. Everything makes the leaves feel slow. You see the motion, so you don't need a pile of describing words in front of it. The verb does the job alone. Try this. Write a line about an object. Then cut every describing word and make the verb carry it. The second time through, listen for the verb in so up and how it tells you to move.
